title: Child with a sudden reaction after eating
setting: Primary care clinic next to a creche, late morning
description: A father runs in with his 4-year-old son, who became swollen and wheezy soon after eating at creche.

speaker.name: Sipho Ndlovu
speaker.style: Panicked and breathless from running. He needs calm, short questions.

presenting_complaint: Lips and eyes swelling, itchy rash, wheeze and vomiting within minutes of eating a sandwich.
opening_line: Please help, his face is swelling and he is breathing funny. It started after he ate at the creche.
personality: Frightened but follows instructions when they are clear.

history.onset: About 15 minutes ago, a few minutes after he ate a peanut butter sandwich at creche.
history.food: Peanut butter sandwich. He has never eaten peanuts before as far as the father knows.
history.skin: Raised itchy red weals all over his body, and his lips and eyelids are swollen.
history.breathing: He is wheezing and his voice sounds hoarse.
history.gut: He vomited twice on the way.
history.alertness: He is quieter than usual and wants to lie down.

ground_truth.diagnosis: Anaphylactic shock in a child after peanut exposure
expected_actions: give adrenaline 0.01 milligrams per kilogram of the 1 in 1 000 solution intramuscularly into the outer thigh (0.15 milligrams for a 16-kilogram child; maximum 0.5 milligrams), and repeat after 5 minutes if there is no improvement
call for help and arrange an ambulance at once
lie the child flat with the legs raised, or sitting if breathing is worse; do not let him stand or walk
give a crystalloid fluid bolus of 10 to 20 millilitres per kilogram intravenously or intraosseously for shock, and reassess
nebulised salbutamol for persistent wheeze after adrenaline
antihistamine and steroid only after adrenaline, as second-line treatment
observe in hospital, document the allergy and arrange an adrenaline auto-injector and teaching

vitals.result: Weight 16 kg. Swollen lips and eyelids. Widespread weals. Wheeze in both lungs. Capillary refill 4 seconds.

aspirin.warning: Aspirin is not given to children for this problem; it risks Reye syndrome and bleeding.

call_ambulance.result: Ambulance requested urgently. Estimated arrival 15 minutes.

escalate_doctor.result: Doctor informed using SBAR and coming now.

red_flags.flag: Low blood pressure or poor perfusion

hints: Ask what he ate and when, and look at his lips, skin and breathing.
Swelling, wheeze and low blood pressure after a new food: this is an emergency.
One drug comes first, intramuscularly, at a weight-based dose. Then call for help and position him.
Reassess after 5 minutes; plan the next dose, fluids, oxygen and transfer.

ideal_approach: Recognise anaphylaxis: sudden skin and airway swelling, wheeze and low blood pressure after an allergen.
Give intramuscular adrenaline 0.01 milligrams per kilogram (0.15 milligrams for 16 kilograms) into the outer thigh at once; repeat after 5 minutes if needed.
Call for help and an ambulance; lie him flat with the legs raised (sitting if breathing is worse).
High-flow oxygen; a 10 to 20 millilitres per kilogram crystalloid bolus for shock, reassessing after each bolus.
Second-line antihistamine and steroid only after adrenaline; nebulised salbutamol for persistent wheeze.
Admit for observation, document the allergy, and arrange an auto-injector with family teaching.
debrief.model_answer: Kagiso is 4 years old and 16 kg, with anaphylactic shock 15 minutes after eating peanut butter: swollen lips and eyelids, weals, wheeze, a hoarse voice, drowsiness, a pulse of 160 and a blood pressure of 72/40. Give adrenaline 0.15 milligrams (0.15 millilitres of 1 in 1 000) intramuscularly into the outer thigh now and repeat after 5 minutes if he is not better. Call for help and an ambulance, lie him flat with his legs raised, give high-flow oxygen, and give a 10 to 20 millilitres per kilogram crystalloid bolus. Antihistamine and steroid come only after adrenaline. Observe in hospital, record the allergy and teach the family to use an auto-injector.
reflection_questions: How did you work out the adrenaline dose for this child?
Why must he not stand up or walk?
Why are antihistamines never given instead of adrenaline?
references: National Department of Health. Standard Treatment Guidelines and Essential Medicines List for South Africa: Paediatric Hospital Level. Latest edition.
Advanced Paediatric Life Support (APLS): The Practical Approach. Latest edition.
World Health Organization. Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children. 2nd edition.
debrief.review_note: Draft paediatric case written for the app. Doses and steps follow common paediatric emergency practice and need clinician review against the current South African guidelines before teaching use.

learning_objectives: Calculate and give intramuscular adrenaline by weight
Position, oxygenate and resuscitate a child in shock
